source_text:
καὶ εἰ νοσοῦμεν, προσφύγωμεν· εἴτε ἀλγοῦμεν
τὴν ψυχήν, τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως ἐξακολουθήσωμεν· εἴτε πεινῶμεν, τὸν ἄρτον δεξώμεθα· εἴτε ἐνεκρώθημεν, τὴν ἀνάστασιν λάβωμεν. εἴτε ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ κατεγηράσαμεν, τὴν σοφίαν παρὰ τῆς σοφίας αἰτησώμεθα. Ἀλλ' ἐξείλκυσεν ἡμᾶς λόγος εἰς μῆκος λόγου. καὶ ἴσως γεγόναμεν ἐμπόδιον πατρικῆς διδασκαλίας. καιρὸς δὲ καλεῖ καὶ μειζόνων ἐπακοῦσαι ῥημάτων, ἵνα ὠφεληθέντες ἐκ μειζόνων ἔργων θεῷ διὰ τῶν ἔργων τὴν δοξολογίαν ἀναπέμψωμεν, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ἀμήν.
thought_title: Closing doxology and appeal to flee to Christ
orientation: Cyril is closing the homily, urging his hearers to flee to Christ for every need and to glorify God through their deeds.
pass_a_gloss: And if we are sick, let us flee to [him]; whether we are in pain in the soul, let us follow after the physician of knowledge; whether we hunger, let us receive the bread; whether we have been put to death, let us take the resurrection. Whether we have grown old in ignorance, let us ask for the wisdom from the wisdom. But the word has drawn us out into length of word. And perhaps we have become a hindrance to the fatherly teaching. But the time calls [us] also to listen to greater words, in order that, having been benefited from greater works, we may send up to God through the works the glorification, to whom [be] the glory both now and always and unto the ages of the ages. Amen.

lemmas.gloss: we have been put to death

choices.why: Keeps the genitive 'of knowledge' literal, preserving the title's ambiguity as the physician who possesses or gives knowledge.

choices.english: we have been put to death
choices.why: Passive aorist of νεκρόω; renders the passive force literally rather than a stative 'we are dead'.
The repetition of σοφία with the article on the second instance suggests personified Wisdom; 'itself' marks the personification without adding a name.

choices.english: a hindrance to the fatherly teaching
choices.why: The genitive after ἐμπόδιον is rendered with 'to', the natural English construction for hindrance.
rejected: an obstacle of the fatherly teaching
a block to the paternal instruction

choices.why: ἀναπέμπω means 'send up'; 'glorification' preserves the noun form of δοξολογία rather than converting to a verb.

pass_b_english: If we are sick, let us flee to him. If our soul is in pain, let us follow the great physician of knowledge. If we hunger, let us receive the bread. If we have been put to death, let us take the resurrection. If we have grown old in ignorance, let us ask wisdom from wisdom itself.

But the word has drawn us out into a lengthy discourse, and perhaps we have become a hindrance to the fatherly teaching. The time now calls us to hear greater words as well, so that, helped by greater works, we may send up glory to God through our deeds. To him be glory both now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

problems.why: Same concept rendered four different ways; reader may not connect them.
problems.fix: Standardize to 'great physician' or add note.

variants.text: the physician and healer of souls and bodies
the physician of souls and bodies

fixed: The source τῷ ἰατρῷ τῆς γνώσεως is rendered 'the physician of knowledge' in the English, which is accurate; the glossary entry for ἀρχιατρός ('great physician') does not appear in this passage, so no standardization is needed here.

polish.changed: Clarified the final doxology by making God the explicit recipient of glory, smoothed the phrase 'ask for wisdom from wisdom itself' to 'ask wisdom from wisdom itself,' and tightened the closing sentence for natural modern rhythm while preserving every claim and qualification.
